A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work, with matching authors, model lineage, datasets and retained benchmark results. Text, equations, figures and tables support comparison. V2 includes Appendix A; the supplied v3 ends after the references despite referring to an appendix. This is an observable omission, not an extraction failure.

before.justification: V2 reports original classification experiments, SECA ablations and accuracy/SOP analyses in Section 5, Tables 2–3 and Figure 3.

after.justification: V3 retains original benchmark and SECA results and reports additional efficiency ablations and temporal accuracy results in Table 2 and Figure 4.

M1.justification: Beyond renaming HM-DF to HD-LIF, v3 introduces an explicit spike-output quantizer Q with bit-width, scaling and rounding controls, separates transmitted spikes from the unquantized reset signal, and incorporates quantization into the backward chain (Equations 4–5). This substantially extends the method; P2-Reset, Mem-BN, SECA, parallel neurons and random backpropagation already existed in v2.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same classification coverage: CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-200, ImageNet-1k and DVS-CIFAR10. Spike precision and parallel-neuron configurations change within these retained tasks.

E2.justification: V2 Table 2 and v3 Table 1 retain the same dataset-specific comparison methods. The efficiency analyses continue using vanilla LIF/online training as the baseline. Newly cited Relaxation LIF and FPTT are discussed but not evaluated as additional comparators.

E3.justification: V3 Table 2 introduces controlled configurations with 4-bit emitted spikes and 50% parallel-neuron substitution. Evaluation expands from accuracy, parameter memory and SOP-based power proxies to reported training seconds per epoch, GPU memory, neuron operations and an mJ energy metric. These are new evaluation configurations; the PDFs do not establish reruns of the retained benchmark experiments.

E4.justification: The new Table 2 isolates spike-compression and parallelization effects on accuracy and training/inference costs, substantially strengthening component analysis. V3 Figure 4 adds temporal comparisons with SECA, while v2 Figure 3's weight-precision-specific SOP sweep is absent. The existing three-dataset SECA ablation remains.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. Random time-step selection is part of the training algorithm, not uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: The benchmark values in v2 Table 2/v3 Table 1 and the SECA results in Table 3 are unchanged. V3 adds substantial efficiency results: its compressed, partially parallel configuration reports 78.61% accuracy, 4.40 MB parameters, 4.62 million NOPs and 0.02 mJ in Table 2. This differs from the retained 78.45% benchmark configuration. Temporal result curves also change, and the earlier weight-specific SOP curves disappear.

T1.justification: Definition 4.1 is reformulated, and Theorem 4.2 changes from sufficient conditions for uniformly firing or silent neurons to gradient-product formulas covering more general firing sequences and an explicit online/STBP gradient relationship. V2's Mem-BN Corollary 4.3 and Appendix A.2 proof are absent from the supplied v3, which provides no corresponding theorem proof.

C1.justification: The central claims of improved gradient separability and efficient online training/deployment remain. V3 shifts emphasis toward quantified inference power and neuron-operation savings: the introduction replaces the 78.45% accuracy/15-fold memory example with 78.61% accuracy, 10-fold memory savings, 11-fold power savings and 30% fewer NOPs.

C2.justification: V3 explicitly acknowledges additional training costs from learnable parameters and explains that vanilla HD-LIF offers no neuron-operation advantage without parallelization. Section 5.4 interprets static-image and event-data temporal behavior as ANN/SNN duality. V2 discusses related temporal observations but lacks these explicit qualifications and interpretation.

D1.justification: V3 adds a code-access link and clarifies some model/block selections. However, the supplied PDF omits v2 Appendix A.1 and Table S1, losing the documented optimizer, scheduler, learning rates, weight decay, augmentation, batch sizes, epochs and configuration mapping. Algorithm 1 is retained in the main text rather than removed. The linked code was not accessed.

R1.justification: V3 adds discussions or citations concerning Relaxation LIF, FPTT with liquid time-constant neurons, and neuromorphic robustness. Five optimizer, scheduler and augmentation references associated with v2's appendix disappear. The broader positioning relative to existing SNN and online-learning approaches remains similar.

P1.justification: V3 retitles the paper, renames the model throughout, rewrites the abstract and contribution summary, reorganizes four method subsections into three, and redistributes the efficiency discussion. It also restructures the experimental analysis, introduces a temporal-processing subsection and moves the pseudocode into the main text.

P2.justification: V3 switches to a two-column layout, adds a radar overview, substantially redraws the model overview, revises block diagrams and introduces a numerical efficiency table. The earlier dual-axis accuracy/SOP figure is replaced by accuracy-only temporal plots. Tables are reformatted, Algorithm 1 is relocated, and the appendix configuration table is absent.

improvement.justification: V3's efficiency ablation and explicit training-cost tradeoffs strengthen evidence for its deployment claims. However, the supplied version loses v2's detailed training recipe and theorem proof while broadening the theorem; the gradient treatment of the new rounded spike outputs also remains unclear. These substantive gains and losses prevent a reliable judgment of net overall improvement.
